resources.string: Shows Wi-Fi networks this phone can see: name, signal strength, frequency band, and the security type each router advertises.

Android limits how often apps can scan, needs Location turned on to return scan results, and may hide some networks. The security type is what the router advertises, not a test of how strong its password is.
Android requires the Location permission to read Wi-Fi scan results. This app does not use your GPS location.
Wi-Fi is turned off. Turn it on and scan again.
Location permission was denied, so scan results cannot be read.
Android returned earlier results because a new scan was throttled or timed out. Wait a minute and scan again.
No networks found. Make sure Wi-Fi and Location are on, then scan again.
Guess based on the network name only. It may be wrong.
Use these guides only for devices and routers you own or are authorised to manage. This app does not read other people\'s networks or passwords.
View a saved Wi-Fi password on your own phone
Android lets you see the password of a network this phone has already joined. It requires your screen lock. Menu names vary by manufacturer and Android version.
Use these steps if you have lost the router admin login or need to restore the router to factory settings.
What this app does not do

This app does not recover, crack, or test Wi-Fi passwords. It has no handshake capture, dictionary or brute-force tools, or deauthentication features. Android does not let apps read other networks\' passwords, and an app cannot verify that you own a network, so such features would be as easy to misuse as to use legitimately. For your own network, use the router admin page, the saved-password steps in Recovery, or contact your ISP. Security professionals test their own equipment with dedicated tools in controlled labs, outside this app.

string-array.name: saved_steps
string-array.item: Open Settings on your phone and search for "Wi-Fi" or "Saved networks".
Open Wi-Fi (or Network & internet, then Internet) and tap the network you are connected to.
Look for a Share or QR-code option.
Confirm with your PIN, pattern, fingerprint or face unlock.
Some phones show the password as text under the QR code; others show only the QR code. Anyone who scans the QR code gets the password, so do not share a screenshot of it.
If the option is missing, the phone may not have saved this network, or the menu is named differently on your phone. Search Settings for "Wi-Fi password" or "Share".

string-array.name: router_steps
string-array.item: Connect to your own network by Wi-Fi or an Ethernet cable.
Find the router address: tap the connected network in Wi-Fi settings and read the "Gateway" value. Common addresses are 192.168.0.1, 192.168.1.1 and 192.168.100.1, but use the one your phone shows.
Open that address in a browser. Some TP-Link models also accept tplinkwifi.net.
Log in with the admin password. If it was never changed, the default is often printed on the router label. If it was changed, use your saved records.
No admin password? Check your password manager, notes, or the setup papers from your ISP. If none of these work, use the factory reset below.

Factory reset: with the router powered on, press and hold the Reset button (usually a small recessed hole) for about 10 seconds until the lights restart. Timing differs by model, so check your manual.
Before resetting, write down your ISP connection details (for PPPoE connections, the username and password from your ISP), any port-forwarding rules, and the Wi-Fi name you use. A reset erases them.

After the reset: log in with the default login on the label, change the admin password, set Wi-Fi security to WPA2-Personal (AES) or WPA2/WPA3, set a new long passphrase, and check for firmware updates.
If the internet does not work after the reset, contact your ISP for the correct connection settings.

string-array.name: learn_wpa_items
string-array.item: WPA2-Personal (PSK) protects the Wi-Fi key with a 4-way handshake and key derivation. It is still widely used. Its strength depends almost entirely on the passphrase: a long random passphrase is strong, while a short or common one is not.

WPA3-Personal (SAE) uses a password-authenticated key exchange designed to resist offline guessing. It needs WPA3-capable devices. WPA2/WPA3 transition mode lets older devices connect, but it is a compromise.
WEP is broken and must not be used. Original WPA with TKIP is obsolete too.
The 2017 KRACK research affected WPA2 implementations. Patched firmware and devices fixed it, which is why router and phone updates matter.

string-array.name: learn_strength_items
string-array.item: Use a random passphrase of at least 16 characters, or 4 to 6 random words, unique to that network.
Avoid the network name, phone numbers, birthdays, family names, and simple patterns such as "bd12345678".
Store the passphrase in a password manager so you never need to memorise it.
Change the passphrase when someone who once had it, such as a former employee, no longer should.

string-array.name: learn_hardening_items
string-array.item: Change the router admin password from the default, and make it different from the Wi-Fi passphrase.
Use WPA2-AES, or WPA2/WPA3 if all your devices support WPA3. Turn off WEP and TKIP-only options.
Disable WPS. Its PIN method is weak.
Keep firmware updated, and enable automatic updates if the router offers them.
Turn off remote administration from the internet unless you need it.
Put guests and smart devices on a separate guest network.
Turn off UPnP unless a specific app needs it, because it lets devices open ports automatically.
Do not put the router brand or model in the network name. Hiding the network name does not provide real security.

string-array.name: learn_weak_items
string-array.item: Default admin logins and default Wi-Fi passwords, especially when printed on labels and shared across many units of the same model.
Outdated firmware with known vulnerabilities, common in old ISP-supplied routers.
WPS enabled, which allows PIN-based attacks.
Open and WEP networks, which offer no real protection.
Short or common passphrases, which can be guessed offline by anyone who has captured the handshake. The defence is a long random passphrase.
Remote administration exposed to the internet.
